now.incomeSrc: Real disposable income per person, Jul–Aug 2026 vs Jul–Aug 2025 (BEA via FRED), the closest match to the Q3-over-Q3 change used for 1950–2022
now.warNote: 21 U.S. deaths (11 in combat) and 865 wounded since Feb 28 (Pentagon, Oct 9–10). Strikes paused; the naval blockade continues. Quinnipiac: 28% approve of the handling of Iran.

fitNote: Approval is Gallup’s pre-election reading for 1946–2022; Gallup stopped publishing it in 2026, so 2026 uses the average of three polling averages. Real income is the change in real disposable income per person, third quarter over third quarter (annual for 1946); for 2026, July–August over July–August. House vote shares for 1946–2000 are Brookings’ (share of all votes), 2002 onward Wikipedia’s, as is 1944 (the baseline for 1946); all are converted to two-party shares.
warNote: The history model asks only whether the U.S. was fighting a war with heavy American losses: hundreds or thousands of U.S. deaths in the election year, as in 1950, 1966, 1970, 2006 and 2010. By that yardstick the Iran war is not one: 21 Americans have died, 11 of them in combat. If it moves the vote, the model would see that through prices and the president’s approval rather than through its war term: gas is up 39% in a year ($2.94 the week before the war began, $4.35 now), and 28% of registered voters approve of the handling of Iran (Quinnipiac, Sept 24–27).

cases.title: Korea, and a strong economy
cases.summary: The Korean War began in June; at least 819 Americans were killed in July alone. Truman’s approval fell to 39%, and Democrats lost 28 seats even though real income per person was up 7.6%. They kept the House.

cases.title: Vietnam escalates
cases.summary: U.S. combat deaths in Vietnam rose from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966, and prices began to climb (3.5% inflation). Johnson’s approval sank to 44%, and Democrats lost 47 seats with unemployment at just 3.7%.

cases.title: Watergate and inflation
cases.summary: Three months after Nixon resigned, inflation was near 12%, gasoline prices were up about a third and real incomes were down 2.3%. Republicans lost 48 seats. Tufte’s approval-and-income model had predicted 60.8% of the two-party vote for Democrats; they won 58.9% by his count (58.5% in this tab’s data).

cases.title: A deep recession
cases.summary: Unemployment reached 10.4% in October and Reagan’s approval was 42%. Republicans lost 26 seats, even though inflation had cooled to 5% and gas was cheaper than a year earlier.

cases.title: Iraq
cases.summary: With 822 U.S. deaths in Iraq that year and Bush’s approval at 38%, Republicans lost 30 seats in a healthy economy (4.4% unemployment, real incomes up 2.3%). District and state studies found larger Republican losses where local casualties were higher.

cases.title: After the Great Recession
cases.summary: With unemployment at 9.4%, Democrats lost 63 seats — more than most published models predicted. The Afghanistan surge peaked the same year, with 437 U.S. combat deaths.

cases.title: Inflation versus Dobbs
cases.summary: Inflation was 8.2% and real incomes fell 3.8%, yet Democrats lost only 9 seats. Half of voters named inflation their top factor and Republicans did better with them; the quarter who named the Dobbs decision voted about 7 to 3 for Democrats.

models.name: Hibbs, Bread and Peace
models.finding: For presidential elections: the incumbent party gains about 3.6 points of vote for each point of real-income growth over the term (weighted toward recent quarters) and loses about 0.3 points per 1,000 U.S. deaths in wars it started. Fitted on 1952–2004; typical miss 2.4 points.

models.name: Tufte, 1975
models.finding: A classic midterm referendum model: the president’s approval and the yearly change in real income per person explained his party’s House vote from 1938 to 1970. It called 1974 within two points.

models.name: Lewis-Beck and Tien
models.finding: House seat change from June approval, election-year income growth and a midterm penalty; typical error about 18 seats.

models.name: Abramowitz
models.finding: Generic-ballot margin plus seats defended: each generic-ballot point is worth about 2.6 House seats. Fitted to the 20 midterms since 1946, it comes within 10 seats in 16; the biggest misses are 1994 and 2006.

models.name: Campbell, surge and decline
models.finding: Midterm losses partly undo the previous presidential year’s surge: the better a party did two years earlier, the more it gives back. This tab’s “previous share” term (the House vote two years earlier) stands in for it.

models.name: Kramer, 1971
models.finding: Economic conditions in the year before an election, led by real personal income, explained about half the variation in the congressional vote from 1896 to 1964.

literature.finding: Public support for the Korean and Vietnam wars fell as cumulative U.S. casualties rose — fastest at first, then more slowly.
Recent casualties matter too, especially when losses are accelerating; the running total alone is an incomplete measure.
literature.source: Gartner and Segura, Journal of Conflict Resolution

literature.finding: By the authors’ estimate, Iraq casualties (dead and wounded) cost President Bush nearly 2 points of the 2004 national vote.
literature.source: Karol and Miguel, Journal of Politics

literature.finding: In 2006, Republican-held House districts swung about 1 point toward Democrats for every two local Iraq deaths.
literature.source: Grose and Oppenheimer, Legislative Studies Quarterly

literature.finding: Republican Senate candidates lost more ground in 2006 where local Iraq casualty rates were higher.
literature.source: Kriner and Shen, Legislative Studies Quarterly

literature.finding: Counterpoint: tolerance for casualties depends mostly on whether the public believes the war is succeeding.
literature.source: Gelpi, Feaver and Reifler, via a review by Paul Musgrave

literature.finding: A 50-cent rise in gas prices within a quarter went with about a 3.5-point drop in presidential approval (1976–2011).
Real gasoline prices help predict presidential approval out of sample.
literature.source: Gupta, Pierdzioch and Tiwari, American Politics Research

literature.finding: Half of midterm voters called inflation the most important factor and Republicans did better with them; about a quarter named the Dobbs decision, and they voted about 7 to 3 for Democrats.
65% of adults say higher-than-usual prices are the result of President Trump’s policies.

info.ai_note: Documented uses of generative AI by campaigns, party committees, officials and foreign operations, with the responses. By the Wesleyan Media Project’s count, pro-Republican sponsors paid for about four in five of the AI-made ads it tracked; examples from both parties are listed.

ai_events.event: Posted an AI-made video of Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer saying profanities he never said, beside House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries in a sombrero, on the eve of the government shutdown.
ai_events.response: Jeffries called it disgusting; a White House spokeswoman called it a perfect meme.

ai_events.event: Posted an AI-made video mocking Vice President JD Vance, one of many AI parodies of the president and his team from the account.
ai_events.response: Reuters called Newsom the most notable Democratic user of AI video.

ai_events.event: Ran an ad in which an AI-made Chuck Schumer speaks a line he was quoted saying in print but never said on camera.
ai_events.response: It carried a small “AI generated” mark; the committee said the words were Schumer’s own.

ai_events.event: Posted an AI parody video showing herself and the president as babies, with “Baby Trump” accused of rigging Texas elections.
ai_events.response: YouTube labeled it altered or synthetic content.

ai_events.event: The Paxton and Cornyn campaigns both used AI videos of their rivals and of Democrats, some with no disclosure.
ai_events.response: Texas has no disclosure law for AI in political ads.

ai_events.event: Ran an 85-second ad with an AI-made James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, reading his old posts along with lines he never said.
ai_events.response: Talarico’s campaign called it a deepfake; the committee said they were his real words.

ai_events.actor: North Star Dawn PAC (alignment not disclosed)
ai_events.event: During the Minnesota Democratic Senate primary, the super PAC’s ad showed Peggy Flanagan in an apparently altered image; she called it a deepfake.
ai_events.response: The PAC called the claim baseless; Minnesota’s deepfake ban is being challenged in court.

ai_events.event: Tested ChatGPT and Google’s AI on election questions. Factual errors fell from about 7–8% of answers in 2025 to none in 2026 tests in Arizona, Michigan and Pennsylvania, but ChatGPT usually gave incomplete candidate lists.
ai_events.response: Fewer than 40% of answers linked to an official state election site.

ai_events.event: Meta removed 35 Facebook and Instagram accounts posing as U.S. activists that posted anti-Republican and immigration memes, some AI-made, to about 79,000 followers.
ai_events.response: Meta says it finds generative AI in virtually every influence network it disrupts.

ai_events.event: Spread celebrity videos with cloned voices, and fake TV reports wearing CNN, BBC and New York Times branding, attacking Democrats and Democratic Senate candidates.
ai_events.response: Fact-checkers rated them false; X, Bluesky and TikTok removed some posts.

ai_events.event: The New York Times reported influence campaigns run end to end by AI agents operating fake-account networks; the Iranian accounts posed as Americans critical of the Republican Party.
ai_events.response: Officials described them as crude but among the first of their kind.

ai_events.event: Ran online ads showing an AI likeness of his challenger, Rebecca Cooke, in invented scenes.
ai_events.response: Cooke’s lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter; Wisconsin’s deepfake law may not reach federal candidates.

ai_events.event: Counted almost 170 AI-made or AI-enhanced political ads, about $80 million of airtime, an undercount. Pro-Republican sponsors ran 80% of them and pro-Democratic sponsors 11%; 69% carried no AI disclaimer.

rules.item: No federal law or FEC rule is written specifically for AI in political ads.
rules.status: The FEC says its ban on fraudulent misrepresentation applies to AI case by case, and it has lacked a quorum since April 30, 2025, so it cannot make rules or open enforcement cases.

rules.item: The FCC’s 2024 proposal to require AI disclosures in broadcast political ads has not been adopted.
rules.status: Its current chairman, Brendan Carr, voted against it.

rules.item: Federal teams that tracked foreign influence were cut back in 2025.
rules.status: The FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force was disbanded, the State Department’s counter-disinformation office closed, and the intelligence community’s Foreign Malign Influence Center is being wound down. Officials called the center redundant; critics said it was being ended in all but name.

rules.item: 33 states have enacted at least one law on deepfakes in election messages, by Public Citizen’s count, which still includes struck-down laws in California and Hawaii and an expired one in Massachusetts.
rules.status: Most require a disclosure rather than a ban. A federal court struck down California’s two laws in 2025; Minnesota’s ban is still being challenged.

rules.item: California and Texas require paid influencers to say a campaign paid them.
rules.status: Federal rules don’t: paid posts on a creator’s own account are exempt.

rules.item: Ended U.S. third-party fact-checking in April 2025 in favor of Community Notes.
rules.status: For 2026 it labels AI content, requires advertisers to disclose AI-made political ads, and takes no new political ads in the final week.

rules.item: Election advertisers must disclose synthetic content, and YouTube labels AI video.
rules.status: In 2025 YouTube offered a way back for creators banned under its retired election-misinformation rules.

rules.item: Allows U.S. political ads again since 2023 and relies on Community Notes rather than professional fact-checkers.
U.S. operations moved in January 2026 to a new joint venture with a majority-American board; the ByteDance algorithm is licensed and is to be retrained on U.S. data.
rules.status: Days later, users said posts about an immigration-agent shooting in Minneapolis were being suppressed; TikTok blamed a data-center power outage.

info.persuasion_note: The strongest recent experiments find that a conversation with an AI moves opinions more than typical ads do in similar tests: about 1.5–4 points on a 0–100 scale in the 2024 U.S. study and about 9–10 in Britain, Canada and Poland, measured right after a chat people agreed to have. About a third of the effect remained a month later, and three in four Americans say they never get news from AI chatbots. Scales differ from study to study, so read each row on its own terms.

persuasion_table.now: +3.9 for the pro-Harris bot among Trump-leaning voters; +1.5 for the pro-Trump bot among Harris-leaning voters
persuasion_table.later: About a third remained a month later

persuasion_table.now: +4.7 during the weeks the ads ran

polling.item: A bot passed 99.8% of quality checks
polling.finding: A Dartmouth study built an AI respondent that mimicked human reading times, mouse movement and typos for about 5 cents an answer. In final-week national polls in 2024, 10 to 52 such fakes could have flipped which candidate led.

polling.item: Bogus respondents are hard to screen out
polling.finding: In a Pew opt-in survey after the 2024 election, 18% of respondents claimed an impossible activity. No screening method removed the bias; probability-based panels were largely unaffected.

polling.item: The pollsters’ code now covers AI
polling.finding: AAPOR’s 2026 code says AI-generated answers are not research participants, and requires pollsters to disclose AI use and whether a sample is probability-based, opt-in or synthetic.
Final-fortnight polls overstated Democratic margins by 2.7 points on average across offices, the third presidential cycle in a row, though their average error fell to 3.3 points from 5.3 in 2020.

polling.item: Most polls had moved online by 2020
polling.finding: AAPOR estimated that 84% of polls before the 2020 election used online methods, up from 56% in 2016; by 2022 a third of national pollsters used probability-based panels.

polarization.measure: House districts that split their tickets in 2024
polarization.trend: 13 Democrats won Trump districts and 3 Republicans won Harris districts, near the post-war low; the 2000s saw five dozen or more per cycle.

polarization.measure: Senate races in 2024 won by the party that lost the state for president
polarization.trend: All four were Democrats in Trump states. Since 2012, 91% of Senate races went the way the state voted for president.

polarization.measure: Correlation of House and presidential margins across districts, 2020
polarization.trend: Close to one-to-one: House races now track the national parties.

polarization.measure: House districts that are highly competitive for president
polarization.trend: About a third were in the 1970s.

polarization.measure: Average warmth toward the other party, 0–100 (2024)
polarization.trend: Down from 48.0 in 1978, while warmth toward one’s own party held near 70.

polarization.measure: Share of 2020 Trump voters who voted for him again in 2024
polarization.trend: 79% of 2020 Biden voters backed Harris. Few switched sides; who turned out mattered more.

polarization.measure: Americans calling themselves independents in 2025, a record
polarization.trend: Even as voting itself stays highly partisan.

Polls from a fake firm were reported as real by several outlets. Kalshi said its markets barely reacted.

landscape.fact: Polymarket paid a $1.4 million penalty to the CFTC for offering unregistered contracts and cut off U.S. users.
A federal judge ruled that the CFTC had exceeded its authority in blocking Kalshi’s contracts on control of Congress.
A French trader put about $30 million on Trump through several Polymarket accounts, raising fears that one bettor could move the odds.
The CFTC dropped its appeal, leaving the ruling for Kalshi in place.
Polymarket bought a CFTC-licensed exchange to return to the U.S.; its U.S. app opened to everyone on the waitlist in May 2026.
CNN, then CNBC, signed data deals with Kalshi. Kalshi and Polymarket together traded more than $45 billion in 2025.
Both exchanges showed Democrats about 51% to win the Senate, the first time Democrats were favored on Kalshi’s contract.
Kalshi fined three congressional candidates for betting on their own races and suspended them for five years.
After a New York Times/Siena poll, Kalshi priced a Republican Senate at 60% and Polymarket at 57%.
By Aug 10, $133 million had been bet on 2026 congressional races, more than in the whole 2024 cycle. On Polymarket, the top 1% of wallets accounted for 68% of the volume.
Kalshi’s “Democrats win both chambers” contract reached a record 58%.
CNN reported more than $750 million traded on 2026 U.S. election markets, as election officials in Los Angeles County and Michigan raised integrity concerns.

Lifetime trading on control of Congress: about 53 million Kalshi contracts on the House and 14 million on the Senate (each pays $1; aggregators report these counts as dollars), and about $16 million and $6 million on Polymarket.
